title: Spread over 3 days, 38 repetitions did the work of 68 crammed ones
body: In 1885 Hermann Ebbinghaus published experiments on his own memory: he learned lists of nonsense syllables and timed how fast he could relearn them later. He forgot fastest at first, about half within an hour and about two-thirds by the next day, and then the curve flattened out. He also found that **38 repetitions spread over three days** worked as well as **68 crammed into one day**. Today this is called the spacing effect: material studied in several separate sessions is remembered better than the same study massed together, one of memory research’s most robust findings.

slides.question: Ebbinghaus crammed a list with 68 repetitions in one day. How many, spread over three days, worked just as well?
slides.explanation: 38 repetitions spread over the three preceding days had just as favourable an effect on relearning as 68 made the day before.

slides.alt: Animation in a ruled notebook: a pencil draws Ebbinghaus’s forgetting curve, steep in the first hours and flat after a day. Then 68 tally marks crammed into one day sit beside 38 spread over three days, with the same result, and a sketch shows each review flattening the curve.

slides.heading: What “savings” means
slides.text: Ebbinghaus measured memory by relearning. If a list took a quarter as long to relearn as it first took to learn, his savings were 75%. Savings of 100% would mean nothing was forgotten.
With any considerable number of repetitions a suitable distribution of them over a space of time is decidedly more advantageous than the massing of them at a single time.

steps.label: Leave a gap: some of it fades
The memory now fades more slowly
So the next review can wait longer

slides.question: How did Ebbinghaus measure what he still remembered?
options: How much faster he could relearn
How many syllables he could write
How long he could recite them
How often he dreamed of them
slides.explanation: He relearned each list and compared the time with the first learning. The time saved, his savings, showed how much of the list was still in memory.

slides.heading: One man’s memory
slides.text: Ebbinghaus was the only subject in his own study, which limits how far it generalises. A 2015 attempt to replicate the forgetting curve, again with one subject, got results similar to his. [Read his chapter on repetition](https://psychclassics.yorku.ca/Ebbinghaus/memory8.htm).
